clue.text: Beautiful sisters from cricketing family?

explanation.surface: Lovely sisters who come from a family famous at cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: The three goddesses of charm in Greek myth were sisters; W. G. Grace headed a celebrated English cricketing family of brothers.

clue.text: Stimulate historian, say

indicators.note: say tells us to hear the name of the historian spoken, not to read its spelling

parts.note: A. L. Rowse was a Cornish historian of Elizabethan England

explanation.surface: Wake up a scholar of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: A. L. Rowse, a well-known British historian, has a surname spoken exactly like the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stimulate someone is to stir or awaken them into activity.

clue.text: Lively record of her sister published in 1992

definitions.text: Lively record of her sister published in 1992

parts.words: Lively record of her sister published in 1992
parts.note: Penelope Lively's novel about the sister of the Egyptian queen points to the queen herself as 'her'

explanation.surface: A vivid account of a woman's sister came out in the early nineties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lively' looks like an adjective but is the novelist Penelope Lively, whose novel named after this queen's sister appeared around then.
explanation.definitionFit: The 'her' whose sister the novel is named after is the famous Egyptian queen.

clue.text: Way up, perhaps, is "arts"

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of is and arts may be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A route upward is, so to speak, the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IS ARTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of steps is a way of climbing up to a higher floor.

clue.text: A blonde I deceived in the library

indicators.note: deceived suggests something led astray, so the letters of the words a blonde I are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to tricking a fair-haired woman inside a library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deceived' rearranges A BLONDE I to give the name of Oxford University's great library.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bodleian is the principal research library of Oxford University.

clue.text: A clip on Scott's James More? (he was in pursuit of Carl Petersen)

definitions.text: he was in pursuit of Carl Petersen

parts.note: a bulldog clip is a strong spring clip for holding papers
James More Drummond, the MacGregor father of Catriona in the Scottish romances, uses the surname Drummond

explanation.surface: A paper clip attached to a Scottish character, with a note about a chase.
explanation.walkthrough: Sapper's hero chased the master criminal Carl Petersen through several thrillers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapper's gentleman adventurer spent several novels hunting the villain Carl Petersen.

clue.text: Poet's twenty-four-hour gun

parts.note: a day lasts twenty-four hours
the Lewis gun was a First World War light machine gun

explanation.surface: A poet owns a weapon that works around the clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Cecil Day-Lewis was Poet Laureate from 1968 to 1972.

clue.text: Part of poem included in The Golden Voice

indicators.note: included in says the letters sit inside the words the golden voice

explanation.surface: A section of verse appears in a celebrated recording by a famous singer.
explanation.definitionFit: The closing stanza addressed to a patron or reader is a short final section of certain poems such as ballades.

clue.text: Completely estimable mother of Tom Jones

parts.note: all can mean entirely or completely
estimable means deserving respect, worthy

explanation.surface: A thoroughly respectable woman is the parent of Fielding's foundling hero.
explanation.walkthrough: In Fielding's novel, the foundling turns out to be the son of Bridget, sister of Squire Allworthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Fielding reveals that the foundling's true parent was Bridget, the squire's sister, who bore that surname.

clue.text: Victorian hero whose agnomen is not at all clear

definitions.text: Victorian hero whose agnomen is not at all clear

parts.words: Victorian hero whose agnomen is not at all clear
parts.note: Hardy's stonemason is known by an added epithet meaning obscure, as in the novel's title

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century protagonist's nickname is very hard to make out.
explanation.walkthrough: An agnomen is an extra name; Hardy's novel styles this hero 'the Obscure'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's novel calls its stonemason hero 'the Obscure', an epithet that means unclear.

clue.text: Roman goodbye to depression

explanation.surface: A Latin farewell to feeling low.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for farewell; also a poetic word for a valley, a low-lying hollow in the land.

clue.text: Nymph may be a butterfly

explanation.surface: A nature spirit might turn out to be an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the nymphs guarding the golden apples in Greek myth; also a skipper, a member of a butterfly family.

clue.text: Country damsel fathomed out by Smollett

definitions.text: Country damsel fathomed out by Smollett

parts.words: Country damsel fathomed out by Smollett
parts.note: the rustic girl seduced by Ferdinand Count Fathom in Smollett's novel, so 'fathomed out' means found out by Fathom

explanation.surface: A rural maiden whose secrets the novelist works out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fathomed' seems to mean understood, but points to Smollett's villain Ferdinand Count Fathom, who seduces this young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the young woman whom Smollett's adventurer Count Fathom seduces.

clue.text: Prepare for publication The Turn of the Tide

indicators.note: the turn of says the word tide is turned round to read the other way

explanation.surface: Getting a book called The Turn of the Tide ready for the press.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends 'The Turn of the Tide' is a title; 'The Turn of' turns TIDE round.
explanation.definitionFit: To revise and correct a text is to ready it for printing.

clue.text: Office of Henley's Brodie

parts.note: Henley and Stevenson wrote a play about Deacon Brodie, so his post is that of a deacon

explanation.surface: The job held by a character in a play by W. E. Henley.
explanation.walkthrough: Henley co-wrote with Stevenson the play 'Deacon Brodie' about an Edinburgh cabinet-maker and burglar.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the rank or post of a deacon, the title Brodie held.

clue.text: Gaunt character of Reade

parts.note: Charles Reade wrote a novel whose title character is surnamed Gaunt, so this is his first name

explanation.surface: A thin, haggard figure from a Victorian novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaunt' looks like an adjective, but it is the surname of the title hero of Charles Reade's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade's 1866 novel takes its title from the full name of its hero, whose first name this is.

clue.text: Some 17s, perhaps, or fellows out of sorts

indicators.note: out of sorts suggests disorder, so the letters of or and fellows are rearranged

explanation.surface: Perhaps a few pupils, or some fellows who feel unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of sorts' rearranges OR FELLOWS.
explanation.definitionFit: Adherents of a teacher, the pupils who come after him, are his disciples.

clue.text: Dick Dudgeon was the devil's

parts.note: Shaw's play names Dick Dudgeon as the devil's follower in its title

explanation.surface: A man in a huff belonged to Satan.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Dudgeon is the hero of Shaw's play 'The Devil's Disciple'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's title calls the hero the devil's follower or adherent.

clue.text: George Washington's horseman

parts.note: a mounted gentleman of Virginia, Washington's home colony, whose settlers were royalist gentry

explanation.surface: The man who rode with the first American president.
explanation.walkthrough: Virginia, Washington's colony, was settled by royalist gentlemen and is nicknamed the Cavalier State.
explanation.definitionFit: A mounted gentleman soldier, and the nickname for Virginia's gentry.

clue.text: Bets on Macaulay's songs

explanation.surface: Wagers placed on the verses of a Victorian historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagers placed; also narrative poems, as in Macaulay's 'Lays of Ancient Rome'.

clue.text: Treacherous boy, born to be king in Lewis

definitions.text: Treacherous boy, born to be king in Lewis

parts.words: Treacherous boy, born to be king in Lewis
parts.note: the Pevensie brother in C. S. Lewis's Narnia betrays his siblings yet later reigns as a king

explanation.surface: A disloyal youngster destined to rule on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lewis' suggests the Hebridean island, but it is C. S. Lewis, whose Narnia boy betrays the others and is later crowned.
explanation.definitionFit: In Narnia the second Pevensie boy betrays his siblings to the White Witch but later becomes a king.

clue.text: Laws of tessellation…

explanation.surface: The rules governing tiled patterns.
explanation.definitionFit: Of Moses, as in the law given to him; also a picture made of small tiles fitted together.

clue.text: Saw a period of publicity

parts.note: an ad is an advertisement, a piece of publicity
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone noticed a spell of advertising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a verb but is the noun for a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, a proverb.

clue.text: … but no law exists here, said Clare

definitions.text: … but no law exists here, said Clare

parts.words: but no law exists here, said Clare
parts.note: the poet John Clare was confined in an asylum, a place he saw as lawless

explanation.surface: A poet remarks that a certain place is lawless.
explanation.walkthrough: John Clare, an English rural poet, spent his last decades in lunatic asylums.
explanation.definitionFit: An asylum is an old name for a mental hospital, a place of chaos.

clue.text: Possibly delivered by boat to De Vries's bird

definitions.text: Possibly delivered by boat to De Vries's bird

parts.words: Possibly delivered by boat to De Vries's bird
parts.note: Peter De Vries wrote a novel titled after a proverb about a goose, and a gravy boat carries a pouring condiment

explanation.surface: Something shipped to a novelist's pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boat' suggests shipping, but it is a gravy boat; Peter De Vries's novel is 'Sauce for the Goose'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravy boat serves a condiment, the very thing that is for the goose in De Vries's title.

clue.text: Long story is again included

indicators.note: included tells us the letters lie inside the words is again

explanation.surface: A lengthy tale is told once more.
explanation.definitionFit: An Icelandic prose epic, or any long rambling account.

clue.text: Pious, cruel, devious friend of Caesar

indicators.note: devious means winding or crooked, so the letters of pious and cruel go astray

explanation.surface: A holy yet cruel and crafty companion of the Roman ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devious' rearranges PIOUS CRUEL into the name of Octavius Caesar's friend in Shakespeare's 'Antony and Cleopatra'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's play he is the follower Octavius sends to Cleopatra.

clue.text: "… view the world as a 10 of tears? / Ah, — sir, not I" (Browning, Confessions)

definitions.text: "… view the world as a 10 of tears? / Ah, — sir, not I" (Browning, Confessions)

parts.words: "… view the world as a 10 of tears? / Ah, — sir, not I" (Browning, Confessions)
parts.note: the missing word is the form of address to a clergyman in Browning's poem 'Confessions'

explanation.surface: A dying man in Browning's poem refuses to see life as gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the missing word; the 10 is VALE, completing 'vale of tears'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the courtesy title used in addressing a clergyman, the priest at the speaker's deathbed.

clue.text: How Henty's characters went to Khartoum

definitions.text: How Henty's characters went to Khartoum

parts.words: How Henty's characters went to Khartoum
parts.note: G. A. Henty's boys' adventure 'The Dash for Khartoum' tells how they hurried there

explanation.surface: The way an adventure writer's heroes travelled to the Sudan.
explanation.walkthrough: G. A. Henty wrote 'The Dash for Khartoum' about the relief of Gordon.
explanation.definitionFit: They went in a rush, hurrying as in the title of Henty's novel.
